text: You get an m by n board of letters and a string, word. Return true if the word can be built from cells that touch up, down, left, or right. Each cell can be used at most once.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I pick any start cell. Then each next letter must sit right next to the last one, and no diagonals. And I can't step on the same cell twice inside one path. Is that right?
Yes. A cell can be reused across different tries, just not within the same path.
Got it. Is the match case-sensitive? The board has upper and lower case letters.
Yes, lowercase a and uppercase A are different.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
m and n are between one and six, and the word length is between one and fifteen. Only English letters.

Okay, so at most thirty-six cells, and the word is short. An exponential search is fine here, as long as I cut dead branches early. The only memory a path needs is which cells it already used, so my state is the cell, the index in the word, and the used set. Quick check on the example board. A, B, C, C, E, D goes straight through, so true. S, E, E is also true. A, B, C, B is false: after A, B, C, the only B next to that C is the one I already used. That's the use-once rule in action.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would list every simple path of length L in the grid and compare each one to the word. Most of those paths are wrong from the very first letter, so it wastes almost all the work. This problem reminds me of backtracking — choose, recurse, undo. I grow the path one letter at a time, and the moment a letter doesn't match, I stop and go back. So I only extend paths that still match a prefix of the word. Breadth-first search fits badly, because every path needs its own used set. Depth-first search keeps one path alive at a time, so I can track used cells on the board itself.

Here's the plan. One: try every cell as a start. Two: compare the letter first — a mismatch is false, and a match on the last letter is true. Three: mark the cell with a hash, try the four neighbours, and if all fail, restore the letter and return false. One thing worth flagging — the mark and the restore are both correctness rules. Without the mark, board A A with word A A A bounces back and forth and says true. Without the restore, board B A A with word A A B keeps hashes from a failed try that block the real path, so it says false. A separate visited grid would keep the input clean but costs m times n extra space, so I'll mark in place. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function tries every cell as a start. The search compares the letter, returns true on the last letter, then marks the cell, tries four directions — skipping cells out of bounds or already a hash — and restores before returning false. One thing worth flagging — the order of the first two checks matters. If I swap them, the last letter is never compared, so board A with word B would say true. Checking for index equals word length at the top breaks too: board A with word A would need a free neighbour to reach that check, so it says false.

Let's dry-run the code with S, E, E — expected true — since it has a real backtrack. The key moment: from the S at row one, column three, I try up first. That E matches, so I mark it, but its only free neighbour is a C. The branch dies, and I restore it to E. Then I go down, then left — the last letter, so true, after fifteen calls. Corner cases: A, B, C, B is false, with every mark undone. A one by one board with word A, A: false. A two by two of all A's with five A's: false — the mark stops reuse. One row A to F with word F, E, D, C, B, A: true, right to left.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is m times n times three to the L. I try every start cell; the first letter has four directions, and after that at most three, because the cell I came from is marked. Space is order L for the recursion stack — marking in place means no visited array. The worst case is a board full of one letter where only the last letter fails. A six by six board of all A's, with fourteen A's then a B, returns false after about four point one million calls — around zero point six percent of the six hundred eighty-eight million bound. Oh, one more thing — when I return true, I don't restore, so the winning path stays as hashes on the caller's board. If the caller needs it again, pass a copy, or restore before returning true.
Good. Follow-up: could you use search pruning to make it faster on a larger board?

Yes, two cheap checks before the search. First, a letter count check: if the word needs more of some letter than the board has, return false right away. In that worst case the board has no B, so it's zero search calls instead of four million. Second, start from the rarer end: if the last letter is rarer on the board than the first, reverse the word. A path exists for the word exactly when one exists for the reversed word, but now the first compare fails fast — B then fourteen A's takes just thirty-six calls, one per cell. Both checks are linear, so they never hurt the big-O. They just kill the worst cases before the exponential part starts.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You used the board itself as the visited set, and you proved both the mark and the restore are needed with tiny counterexamples. You caught that a true return leaves hashes on the caller's board. And for the follow-up, you had concrete numbers: the letter count check turns four million calls into zero, and reversing turns them into thirty-six. Good work.
